subtitle: Intercultural competence means turning curiosity, understanding and communication skills into thoughtful action across differences. This course shows what that looks like in everyday work.
scope: For staff across DHS. Use practice or nonsensitive examples. Activities develop practical skills and do not administer the IDI, assign individual orientations, certify competence or replace formal requirements and employee protections. Matters involving Native American communities or Tribal relations should be referred to the appropriate office within ADSA.
introTranscript: Intercultural competence involves understanding and responding across perceived cultural differences, including learned meanings of respect, appreciation, belonging and disagreement. It is more than a friendly intention or a repair to unclear instructions. This course follows Casey and Morgan, who learned different meanings of public recognition through family and community experience. You will examine your own interpretation, ask a proportionate question and use the clarified meaning to choose an appropriate response. Personal understanding and thoughtful work are both worthwhile; no account needs to be privately disclosed or used to assign an IDI orientation.

intro.heading: Connect understanding to action
intro.body:
Intercultural competence brings attitudes, understanding and skills into action across perceived cultural difference. A clear instruction may be useful, but intercultural learning also asks what a response means in a person’s learned context. A welcoming intention does not establish that the meaning was understood.

In a DHS team, Morgan thanks Casey publicly by naming Casey alone as the reason a shared activity succeeded. Morgan learned through familiar family and community experience that individual public praise communicates sincere appreciation. Casey responds quietly and later says the thanks felt uncomfortable. Morgan initially reads that response as rejection or lack of gratitude.

Casey voluntarily offers a broad explanation: in experiences meaningful to Casey, recognition shows respect when it includes people whose contributions made the work possible. Being singled out felt as if their effort had disappeared. Casey is explaining a personally learned meaning, not describing everyone with a similar name, appearance or affiliation. Morgan’s and Casey’s accounts need not be ranked as better or worse.

A thoughtful response connects this understanding to action. Morgan can acknowledge the actual shared contributions appropriately and offer suitable individual thanks without dismissing either value. Formal performance records or decisions retain their actual standards and processes. The exercise illustrates culturally informed inquiry and response; it does not assess either person or certify an IDI orientation.

items.title: Intention and culturally learned meaning
items.body: Morgan’s public praise is meant sincerely, but its familiar meaning is not automatically Casey’s meaning. The volunteered account reveals why being singled out felt uncomfortable. Examine both learned interpretations rather than declaring one person ungrateful or assuming the same response for everyone associated with Casey.

items.title: Understanding changes the response
items.body: Morgan can name the actual shared contribution and choose an appropriate way to offer individual appreciation. The change follows Casey’s expressed meaning of respect, rather than just clarifying an instruction. It should not erase Casey’s achievements or invent an exception to formal records and performance processes.

items.title: A practice account with a limit
items.body: The family and community experiences in this case are invented influences on two individuals. They provide a way to explore cultural meaning without requiring a personal history from learners. A private reflection on your own meaning of appreciation is valid, and neither the scenario nor disclosure provides an IDI result.

tabs.label: Good intention only
tabs.body: Good intention explains Morgan’s purpose but does not settle Casey’s meaning. Repeating the praise more emphatically could intensify the same misunderstanding. Ask a suitable question and use the expressed account, rather than assuming sincere thanks must be experienced identically across learned perspectives.

tabs.label: Meaning and action
tabs.body: Meaning and action connect Casey’s volunteered explanation to a different response. Morgan can accurately include collaborators and choose suitable individual thanks. This is not merely making instructions clearer: it responds to learned meaning while retaining the actual work and formal responsibilities.

tabs.label: Personal label
tabs.body: A personal label may sound decisive but exceeds what one activity can establish. Course practice is not an individual IDI assessment or a personnel standard. Describe the action, its effect and the next improvement instead of assigning cultural status to the learner.

wrong: Morgan’s sincere intention proves every form of praise feels the same to everyone.
Casey’s response proves everyone with a presumed shared identity rejects praise.

check.feedbackCorrect: The account connects a culturally learned meaning to a changed response while preserving individual variation and assessment limits.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Sincere intention does not establish another person’s meaning. A single response cannot predict a whole group. One changed exchange cannot certify an IDC orientation. Describe the expressed perspective and the purposeful response, with actual standards and uncertainty retained rather than a personal or group label.

intro.heading: Practice openness without abandoning judgment
intro.body:
Openness includes being willing to learn a meaning that differs from your familiar interpretation. It does not require agreeing with every action or asking someone to explain an entire cultural identity. A suitable question gives the person room to describe what matters in the particular exchange.

In the practice recognition case, Morgan could ask whether the way thanks was offered left something important out. Casey can choose whether to answer. The question should not accuse Casey of ingratitude or demand a family history. If Casey gives a broad explanation about shared contribution, Morgan can examine that meaning alongside the familiar individual-praise expectation.

A learner can instead explore the practice account or privately reflect on a chosen meaning of respect. No personal explanation needs to be entered or shared. Curiosity becomes intrusive if it makes a person represent everyone with a presumed affiliation, or treats optional disclosure as a condition of receiving recognition.

Keep actual standards and boundaries. Understanding why a form of appreciation matters does not authorize changing formal performance records or waiving a duty. A respectful response may include a reasoned limit where necessary. Openness keeps inquiry revisable while actual decision authority and required processes remain clear.

items.title: A question can reveal meaning
items.body: Ask whether the recognition left something important out and allow Casey to correct the interpretation. The answer may concern learned respect for shared contribution, not lack of gratitude. This opens a culturally meaningful inquiry without requiring a full identity story or assuming a motive from the initial response.

items.title: Curiosity does not require biography
items.body: Morgan need not ask Casey to explain a family, community or nationality to the team. The broad volunteered meaning can be enough for this situation. Learners may use the practice account or private reflection instead, keeping choice real without making a person a compulsory teaching resource.

items.title: A boundary remains meaningful
items.body: Recognition should accurately describe the actual contributions. Morgan can understand Casey’s learned meaning while keeping formal performance standards and records in their appropriate process. If a proposed acknowledgment invents credit or erases an achievement, explain the limit and consider another respectful expression; openness does not require approval of an inaccurate account.

tabs.label: Close the inquiry
tabs.body: Closing inquiry with an ingratitude label treats Morgan’s learned meaning as universal. It prevents Casey’s account from informing the response. Ask a suitable question about the appreciation and its meaning before concluding that the person rejects thanks or is a representative of a group style.

tabs.label: Agree automatically
tabs.body: Automatic agreement could treat any suggested recognition as appropriate without checking accuracy or role responsibility. Understanding Casey’s meaning does not authorize inventing collaborators’ work, hiding Casey’s achievement or altering formal records independently. Consider suitable appreciation grounded in the actual contribution, with a reasoned limit where a proposal exceeds the role.

tabs.label: Ask proportionately
tabs.body: A proportionate question concerns this recognition and leaves Casey choice about explanation. A broad answer may reveal how respect and contribution were understood. Use that meaning while avoiding a personal-history demand and keeping formal recognition or employment decisions with their actual standards and processes.

check.question: Which question opens the practice recognition exchange appropriately?

wrong: Why are people from your presumed background always ungrateful?

check.feedbackCorrect: The question opens a meaning that could revise Morgan’s interpretation without demanding identity disclosure or changing formal standards.
check.feedbackIncorrect: The first claim stereotypes and assigns motive. A whole-community explanation makes recognition conditional on representation. Removing formal standards bypasses actual responsibility. Ask about this exchange, preserve choice and use any volunteered meaning without turning it into a group rule or automatic approval.

intro.heading: Use knowledge without making a person predictable
intro.body:
Knowledge can help you recognize that a familiar meaning is learned rather than universal. Cultural meanings of respect, recognition and participation can vary across settings and within communities. A general reference can open a question, but cannot tell you what a particular person means or identify their preferences from appearance.

In the practice recognition case, Morgan reads about the possibility that appreciation can emphasize individual or shared contribution. That gives Morgan another question to consider. It does not prove what Casey wants. Casey’s volunteered account of a learned meaning, the actual shared work and the present setting remain more relevant than a memorized group profile.

Do not turn Casey’s account into a new rule for everyone with an assumed affiliation. Another person may prefer individual public acknowledgment, and Casey’s meaning may vary by context. Role, privacy, the contribution and formal requirements also matter. Culturally informed inquiry considers these together rather than explaining everything through one category.

Choose a suitable source for a defined question and retain its limit. Educational concepts can support private reflection or practice learning. Actual employment and record requirements need their authoritative sources and responsible processes. Knowledge becomes a useful part of competence when it helps you listen and ask more carefully, not when it supplies a script for another person.

items.title: Knowledge opens a meaning question
items.body: A conceptual distinction between individual and shared contribution can help Morgan recognize another possible meaning of thanks. It remains a possibility rather than Casey’s answer. Ask proportionately and use the person’s volunteered explanation, without requiring that the explanation match a source or a group profile.

items.title: An individual account has context
items.body: Casey describes one learned meaning important in this exchange. That does not establish every future preference or every community member’s practice. Ask whether the response fits this contribution and setting. Role, privacy and actual records responsibilities remain relevant alongside cultural meaning.

items.title: A source has a proper use
items.body: An educational reference can support conceptual understanding. A formal requirement needs its actual authoritative source and appropriate interpretation. Keep those uses distinct so a helpful reading does not become invented permission, a Minnesota mandate or a test of an individual’s cultural identity.

tabs.label: Memorized profile
tabs.body: A memorized profile may tell Morgan what Casey is supposed to want before Casey speaks. It can miss variation, context and the actual contribution. Use knowledge to widen the meaning question rather than predicting the person’s answer from an assumed background or treating a source as a personal assessment.

tabs.label: Defined source question
tabs.body: A defined question helps select the relevant kind of source. A cultural concept may support learning; a decision requirement needs its authoritative material. This keeps knowledge useful and limits the temptation to use one familiar source as the answer to every work issue.

tabs.label: Knowledge plus inquiry
tabs.body: Knowledge plus inquiry lets Morgan notice another possible meaning and then listen to Casey’s voluntary account. The response can address shared contribution without making it a universal group rule. This connects conceptual knowledge with individual context, culturally informed understanding and appropriate actual responsibility.

check.feedbackCorrect: General knowledge informs inquiry without becoming an individual conclusion or operational authority.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A group description cannot prove an individual preference. It cannot authorize bypassing a requirement or settle an accommodation issue. Define the question, use the appropriate source and examine relevant context before choosing a response.

intro.heading: Check culturally learned meaning before acting on your interpretation
intro.body:
A quiet response to thanks is observable; ingratitude is an interpretation. Morgan’s learned association between individual public praise and sincere respect made the response seem puzzling. To examine it, Morgan needs a question that can reveal another meaning rather than simply confirm the initial story.

In the practice exchange, Casey voluntarily explains that shared contribution matters in how respect is expressed. Morgan can restate the account neutrally: you valued the appreciation, but being singled out felt as though collaborators’ effort was left out—is that what you mean? Casey may correct or limit the account. This is a practice individual meaning, not a profile of a community.

AHRQ’s check-back reference concerns communication confirmation in healthcare. The course adapts only its basic restatement-and-correction idea to an invented administrative exchange. It does not import clinical directions or suggest that confirmation alone supplies cultural understanding. Here the important content is Casey’s learned meaning and Morgan’s willingness to examine their own frame.

Use the correction. Morgan can stop treating Casey as ungrateful and consider accurate shared acknowledgment plus suitable individual thanks. A learner can also privately explore how their own meaning of respect shaped an interpretation. Actual records and performance decisions remain governed by their standards and responsible process, and the exercise establishes no IDC placement.

items.title: The initial frame
items.body: Morgan has experienced public individual recognition as respectful. That learned frame helps explain the ingratitude interpretation but does not make it true. Name both the observable response and your added meaning so the inquiry can genuinely change the account rather than defend the first explanation.

items.title: A restatement that permits correction
items.body: Restate Casey’s account of shared contribution without claiming that all members of a community feel the same. Ask whether the account fits and allow correction or refusal of further personal explanation. The useful result is a more accurate understanding of this exchange, not a forced identity narrative.

items.title: The correction changes the next step
items.body: Once Morgan understands that shared effort seemed absent, repeating the same praise is not the only option. Morgan can acknowledge the real collaborators and offer appropriate individual thanks. This response follows a changed cultural meaning while keeping actual achievements and formal responsibilities intact.

tabs.label: Confirm the first story
tabs.body: A question such as why are you ungrateful embeds the initial interpretation and may push Casey to defend against it. It does not open the meaning. Describe the quiet response and invite an optional explanation about this recognition, rather than demanding agreement with Morgan’s learned frame.

tabs.label: Check the expressed meaning
tabs.body: A neutral restatement tests the account Casey volunteered and allows correction. Morgan need not adopt a universal group theory or require a private biography. The check becomes interculturally meaningful because it concerns a learned understanding of respect and contribution, rather than only an unclear procedural instruction.

tabs.label: Use the changed account
tabs.body: Using the changed account means revising the motive interpretation and choosing a response that fits the expressed meaning. Accurate shared acknowledgment may become appropriate. The change does not certify Morgan’s competence or authorize altering performance records; it illustrates perspective and response within actual responsibility.

check.question: Which response best checks the practice meaning of Casey’s quiet reaction?
check.correct: Restate Casey’s expressed concern about omitted shared contribution, invite correction and revise the response while keeping formal responsibilities clear.
wrong: Ask Casey to confirm that the reaction was ungrateful.
Record the explanation as a universal rule for a presumed community.
Thank Casey for explaining but continue treating the reaction as rejection.
check.feedbackCorrect: The response invites correction of a culturally learned meaning and uses the account rather than merely listening politely.
check.feedbackIncorrect: An ingratitude prompt forces the first frame into the question. A universal community rule exceeds Casey’s account. Polite listening without revising the response preserves the original misunderstanding. Check the expressed meaning, allow correction and connect it to an appropriate action without assessment or authority claims.

intro.heading: Adjust your response without stereotyping or imitating
intro.body:
The official IDC associates Adaptation with culturally informed perspective shifting and a suitable change in behavior. This is more specific than changing any instruction or making any convenient adjustment. The practice recognition example examines the relationship between learned meaning, a revised frame and an appropriate response; it cannot establish that anyone holds the orientation.

Morgan initially treats individual public praise as the obvious expression of appreciation. Casey’s volunteered meaning shows how that form could seem to erase shared effort. Morgan can understand the recognition from that perspective and change the response: accurately acknowledge collaborators and choose a suitable way to thank Casey individually. The change addresses expressed meaning rather than merely an information gap.

Do not imitate a guessed identity, exaggerate a greeting or make Casey responsible for a group profile. Nor should Morgan invent achievements for collaborators, hide Casey’s contribution or alter formal employment records outside assigned authority. Respectful recognition and accurate responsibility belong together. Ask whether the proposed response fits this contribution and setting.

A person’s meaning can vary, so the revised approach is not a permanent script for Casey or others. Private reflection on your own meaning of respect can also be a worthwhile outcome without an operational result. The official continuum ends with Adaptation as its fifth orientation; in this program, Integration means the people a process affects help design it, and it is not a sixth official orientation.

items.title: A culturally informed shift
items.body: Morgan recognizes that respect can mean making shared contribution visible, not only naming an individual publicly. That perspective shift changes which response seems appropriate in the exchange. The course illustrates this relationship without converting one thoughtful response into an assessment result or a universal group preference.

items.title: An appropriate behavioral response
items.body: Morgan can include actual collaborators and offer individual thanks in a suitable way after checking the expressed meaning. This differs from copying a supposed cultural style: the action addresses Casey’s account and the real contribution. It should remain accurate rather than invent credit to create a pleasing performance.

items.title: Formal standards remain
items.body: A workplace recognition conversation is not permission to change formal performance records or required criteria. Keep those decisions in their proper process and role. A response can respect the expressed meaning while accurately recording achievements, preserving employee protections and avoiding an unsupported waiver of duties.

tabs.label: Ordinary adjustment
tabs.body: An ordinary adjustment may clarify an instruction or improve convenience, which can be useful. It does not automatically show a culturally informed frame shift. In this case, identify the different learned meanings of respect and how understanding them changes the recognition, without implying that every work repair assesses Adaptation.

tabs.label: Culturally informed response
tabs.body: A culturally informed response uses the expressed meaning to reconsider a familiar frame and act appropriately. Morgan sees how individual praise could obscure shared effort and chooses accurate shared acknowledgment plus suitable thanks. This is a bounded practice illustration, not certification of an orientation or a group rule.

tabs.label: Identity imitation or waiver
tabs.body: Identity imitation or a formal waiver can look flexible while missing the meaning or responsibility. A guessed group performance imposes a stereotype; altered employment records may exceed authority. Choose a response tied to Casey’s account, actual contribution and appropriate process rather than displaying culture or ignoring standards.

A guessed identity greeting proves understanding even if Casey’s account is ignored.
Meaningful recognition authorizes changing formal employment records independently.
check.feedbackCorrect: The response connects a culturally learned perspective with appropriate behavior while preserving evidence and authority limits.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A procedural improvement alone cannot certify an orientation. A guessed identity performance ignores the expressed meaning. Recognition does not grant authority over formal records. Name the culturally informed frame shift and suitable action, keeping accuracy, individual variation and actual process boundaries visible.

intro.heading: Use feedback to plan the next practice
intro.body:
Useful feedback can identify how a learner examined culturally learned meaning and changed a response. Morgan asked about appreciation, checked Casey’s explanation of shared contribution and considered accurate recognition. That feedback is more specific than calling Morgan culturally aware. It describes the reasoning and action without assessing the person.

A personal-understanding gain is also legitimate. A learner may privately notice how family or community experience shaped what respect or thanks means to them. They can retain the question without a public account or workplace metric. Use the Casey and Morgan example whenever preferred; no personal story needs to be entered or shared.

For an optional work practice, choose a suitable next exchange and ask whether your familiar meaning is being assumed as universal. Use a proportionate inquiry if needed and examine how the account changes the response. If the result is unexamined, keep it open. Formal responsibilities and employee protections continue rather than becoming a test of how flexible you appear.

Course answers, feedback or one changed recognition cannot determine an IDI orientation or complete intercultural development. The next inquiry may involve another meaning or context. Consultant knowledge and feedback can help staff reflect and prepare their work, while the personal insight and actual work ownership remain with the learner.

inThisLesson: Write specific feedback about the culturally learned meaning and response in a practice exchange.
Choose a meaningful personal inquiry or observable work practice with an appropriate boundary.
Distinguish a development plan from a personal rank or complete competence claim.
Which next plan is appropriate?
lessons.keyStatement: Make the next practice specific enough to learn from.

items.title: Feedback names meaning and response
items.body: Morgan checked the shared-contribution meaning and changed the recognition appropriately. This identifies what was learned and what action followed. It does not imply that every future appreciation should use the same method, or certify the whole person. Specific feedback leaves the next contextual question open.

items.title: Personal growth without proof of work
items.body: A learner can notice that a valued family practice shaped their sense of respect and explore another possible meaning privately. That insight has value even without a work application. If something is shared, use broad nonsensitive or invented material rather than requiring a private family narrative to demonstrate depth.

items.title: A bounded next practice
items.body: In another invented exchange, ask what your familiar meaning assumes and whether a suitable inquiry is needed. Examine how any clarified account affects the next response. Retain unknown results and actual responsibilities; do not turn the practice into a hidden employee score or claim complete competence.

tabs.label: General praise
tabs.body: General praise such as culturally aware can encourage a learner but does not identify the meaning examined or response improved. Add a specific description of the perspective and action. This makes feedback useful without implying that one exchange supplies a cultural rank or comprehensive personal assessment.

tabs.label: Specific next inquiry
tabs.body: A specific next inquiry asks where another learned meaning might change the response. It may concern private personal understanding or an appropriate work exchange. Neither route requires a public story, and the personal path needs no work-proof metric. Keep the question purposeful and responsive to context.

tabs.label: Personal ranking
tabs.body: A personal ranking shifts feedback from the practiced action to an unsupported developmental claim. Participation and course answers do not administer the IDI or establish a personnel standard. Keep learning feedback separate from formal assessment and from the actual responsibilities governing employment decisions.

check.question: Which next learning step fits the practice recognition case?
check.correct: Explore how learned meanings of respect shaped the interpretation, privately or through the practice case, and optionally practice a suitable response without claiming an IDI result.
wrong: Treat the clarified meaning as a permanent rule for everyone with a presumed identity.
Declare complete competence after one exchange.
Accept personal reflection only when it produces an operational metric.
check.feedbackCorrect: The step values culturally meaningful understanding and optional response practice without a group script, assessment claim or work-proof gate.
check.feedbackIncorrect: An individual meaning is not a permanent group rule. One exchange does not complete competence or establish an IDI result. Personal reflection does not need an operational metric to matter. Examine the learned meaning, choose an appropriate inquiry or response and retain individual variation, context and actual responsibilities.

items.text: Privately examine what public appreciation means to you, or use the example.
Choose appropriate recognition after checking Casey’s expressed meaning.
Does the response fit this contribution and setting?
Which part of the response’s effect remains unexamined?
Casey’s meaning predicts everyone with a presumed identity.
One exchange proves complete intercultural competence.

lessons.next: Use openness, relevant knowledge and practical skills together, then learn from the action and its effect.

scenario.context: DHS practice case: Morgan used Casey’s volunteered learned meaning to revise recognition. A learner also gains a private insight into their own meaning of appreciation. A facilitator wants to certify everyone’s IDC placement.
options: Rank participants from their disclosures or exercise results.
Recognize the personal insight or specific meaning-to-response practice, choose another inquiry and keep actual assessment separate.
Apply Casey’s account as a permanent rule for every group member.
responses: Neither disclosure nor exercise results administer the IDI.
This values personal growth and culturally informed practice with honest limits.
The practice individual account does not supply a universal group script.

lessons.transfer: Privately reflect on a learned meaning of respect or use Casey and Morgan. Optionally describe specific feedback and a next practice, without entering sensitive personal material.

move.control: You can use specific feedback and appropriate guidance to improve your next work response.
move.failure: Learning becomes a broad self-certification or a ranking of other people.
move.next: Choose another culturally meaningful question and keep personal or work learning bounded.

jobAid.subtitle: Connect culturally learned meaning with understanding and an appropriate response.
remember: A friendly intention or clearer instruction alone is not the whole of intercultural competence.
In this example, a person’s learned meaning is an individual account, not a community profile.
Private personal understanding is worthwhile; course practice cannot establish an IDI orientation.

sections.heading: Understand meaning
items: Describe the observed response and your culturally learned interpretation separately.
Ask a suitable optional question that can reveal another meaning.
Use knowledge to open inquiry rather than predict a person.
Allow private reflection or a practice alternative without required entered accounts.

sections.heading: Connect perspective and response
items: Explain how the volunteered meaning changes your familiar frame.
Choose an appropriate action tied to the person’s account and actual context.
Preserve accurate contribution, employee protections and formal responsibilities.
Avoid identity imitation, universal scripts or an assessment claim.

sections.heading: Learn and continue
items: Value a more nuanced personal understanding without a work metric.
For work practice, name the specific action, evidence and unexamined result.
Choose another inquiry and use consultant guidance without giving up ownership.

sources.title: Council of Europe: Developing intercultural competence through education
sources.note: Pages 16–21 provide the conceptual definition and action component; this course’s cases, goals and practice feedback are newly authored applications, not a reproduced assessment.

sources.title: IDI: Intercultural Development Continuum
sources.note: Official five orientations ending with Adaptation. The course does not administer or infer individual assessment results; program Integration means the people a process affects help design it.

sources.title: AHRQ TeamSTEPPS: Check-Back
sources.note: Provides a limited reference for restating and confirming meaning in communication. The administrative example does not import clinical instructions or certify understanding of every cultural question.

sources.title: DHS Equity Policy
sources.note: DHS equity and learning context; optional practice does not replace required learning, formal analysis or responsible operational processes.
